store.2: I am currently working in an interdisciplinary lab where computer scientists collaborate with experts from various fields such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience. Our goal is to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. I am responsible for developing front-end prototypes that present slices of data in interactive dashboards. This involves using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering when dealing with 3D data.
store.3: My first research project involved visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. The project involved aggregating and presenting daily temperature readings from buoys across the Pacific. I wrote scripts to clean and unify the data, built a pipeline for near real-time updates, and designed interfaces for researchers to explore specific regions or timeframes. This experience led to co-authoring my first paper on the system, which was a surreal and proud moment. I hope to continue exploring and learning through research.
store.4: Currently, my research has shifted towards immersive analytics platforms, exploring how VR or AR technologies can enhance scientists' understanding of complex data. By providing an intuitive, interactive experience, immersive analytics can revolutionize the way data is analyzed. It's exciting to be at the forefront of this cutting-edge field, where each day brings new challenges and opportunities to forge new paths. The integration of VR headsets, collaboration with game engines like Unity or Unreal, and efficient data streaming into 3D environments are just a few aspects of this innovative work. It's a thrilling experience to be part of this pioneering effort.
store.5: Research life is often misunderstood as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away on a mysterious project. However, it involves a lot of reading, including academic papers. When solving a bug with rendering volumetric data in VR, I need to find similar attempts in conference proceedings or workshops. It can be overwhelming, but over time, I've learned to skim through papers by reading the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to determine relevance. Occasionally, when I find something interesting, I share it with the lab, and we discuss how to incorporate that technique into our workflow. It's a collaborative process that helps us improve our methods.
store.6: I have the opportunity to interact with graduate students, both master's and PhD candidates, in the lab. Initially, it can be intimidating to engage with them due to their deep expertise in their respective fields. However, it is also inspiring to see their dedication and passion for their research. One PhD student is developing a machine learning algorithm for on-the-fly compression of large datasets and integrating it with our VR platform. This concept is fascinating as it aims to improve real-time performance by using compressed representations of data, such as climate datasets, until a closer zoom is required. Collaborating with him allows me to witness the practical application of advanced theoretical concepts. Informal brainstorming sessions often occur in the lab break room, where we discuss innovative ways to optimize processing by leveraging the GPU. These interactions are valuable for learning and driving progress in our research.
store.7: I have added your experience with poster presentations at smaller symposiums to the core memory. It was a great opportunity to distill complex research into easy-to-understand visuals and talking points. Initially, I was nervous about presenting, but it turned out to be a friendly dialogue with genuine interest from the audience. Even industry professionals and local startup representatives attended, sharing valuable insights on how VR for data visualization could be applied in marketing analytics and architecture. This experience opened my eyes to the potential real-world applications of research beyond academia.
store.8: I have added your experience with co-authoring workshop papers and working on a conference submission to the core memory. Currently, I am co-authoring a paper for the IEEE Visualization Conference(IEEE VIS), which focuses on a user study comparing traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers identify anomalies or trends faster than 2D charts. We conducted a small user trial with 15 participants, recorded their times, and asked them to complete a UX questionnaire. Now, we are analyzing the data to determine if there is a statistically significant difference. The paper is a collaborative effort, with each co-author contributing their expertise. It requires a delicate balance, especially considering my senior coursework and capstone project. I hope to see the paper through to completion.

By incorporating new findings, exploring alternative angles, or applying existing concepts in innovative ways, we can push the boundaries of research. The collaborative nature of research, both within our lab and among the global community, is truly special. It's a testament to the collective pursuit of knowledge and the advancements that can be made through shared efforts.

We learned from the experience and implemented new measures to prevent such a crisis in the future. It's a valuable lesson in the importance of data management and the need for redundancy in our systems.

I had the opportunity to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics, where I met experts from around the world discussing technical details, proposing new frameworks, and engaging in lively debates. Witnessing the cutting-edge of CS knowledge in real-time was truly fascinating. This experience has broadened my understanding and inspired me to continue exploring the field.
